# Journey: diagnosing a stale node

**The symptom.** A node's value is out of date. Something upstream moved, or you sent a message, and the node did not re-run — or it ran and produced what it produced last time.

**The answer, up front.** Six things stop a node from re-running: no subscription edge, an unmatched `when:` predicate, a failed-terminal marker left on the node, a cascade mode that dropped the round, a sender that never ran in this frame, and a paused instance. Each has a distinct read. Work down the list.

```
ID=<instance-id>
API=http://127.0.0.1:8080
```

## 1. Read the node's whole state

Get the node id, then read the node:

```
rimsky instance nodes $ID
curl -s "$API/v1/nodes/<node-id>" | jq
```

The route answers with the node's id, instance, type, executor, declared tags, cascade mode, creation time, the run tallies, `latest_attributes` — the attribute bag the last run left behind — and `settling_signal_type`, the marker naming how it settled.

`rimsky node get <node-id>` renders a narrower projection of the same document: identity, executor, run tallies, and the settled signal, without the tags, the cascade mode, or the attributes. Reach for the route when you need the attributes.

Two fields decide where you go next. `settling_signal_type` starting with `terminal/error/` sends you to section 4. Run tallies that did not change across the event you expected to wake it send you to section 2.

## 2. Is there an edge at all?

**Subscribing is waking.** Every `subscribes:` entry marks this node stale on a matching emission and gates its dispatch on the sender. There is no declaration that reads a sender's data without also waking on it — and, equally, no wake without a declaration.

Check the template for an entry naming the sender and a type that its emission matches:

| You want to wake on | Write |
| --- | --- |
| The sender settling successfully | `type: terminal/success` |
| The sender settling any way | `type: terminal/*` |
| A specific value the sender wrote | `type: attribute/<key>/changed` |
| Any value the sender wrote | `type: attribute/*` |
| An error family | `type: terminal/error/http/*` |

An `attribute/<key>/changed` signal fires when the sender wrote a value for `<key>` that **differs from the same node's prior run in the same run-scope**. A sender that recomputes the same value emits nothing, and a receiver waiting only on that signal correctly does not run.

## 3. Did the predicate match?

A `when:` predicate that evaluates false is a silent non-wake, and so is one that **errors** — an evaluation error is treated as no-match.

Read what the sender actually emitted:

```
curl -s "$API/v1/events?instance_id=$ID&kind=work_completed" | jq '.events[] | {node_id, payload}'
```

Then check your predicate against that payload. `terminal/success` carries `changed`, `attributes_delta`, `change_summary`, and `tags`. `terminal/error/<class>` carries `error_class`, `error_payload`, `attempt`, `retries_so_far`, `attributes_delta`, and `tags`. `attribute/<key>/changed` carries `key`, `value`, and `old_value`.

A predicate reading a field that is absent from the payload is the usual mistake. Under an exact `type:` the field is checked at registration; under a wildcard `type:` it is not, and an absent field surfaces only as a node that never wakes.

## 4. Is a failed-terminal marker sitting on the node?

A node that settled failed carries that marker, and it stays eligible-blocked until you clear it.

```
rimsky admin reset <node-id>
```

The verb takes a **node** id — an instance id answers `404 node not found` — and clears the failed-terminal settling-signal marker so the node becomes eligible again. Afterwards the same read reports the node with no settled signal at all, while its id, its executor, its run tallies, and the attributes the failed run left behind are unchanged. The clearing appears in the instance's event log as one `operator_override` entry.

Two refusals are worth knowing. The route answers `409 reset only valid when node has a failed terminal run in some scope` on a node that never failed. And the reset performs **no state transition and no re-dispatch** — it makes the node eligible; something still has to wake it.

## 5. Did the cascade mode drop the round?

`cascade_mode` governs what happens when a second round targets a node that already has a round in the current frame.

| Mode | What it does to an earlier round |
| --- | --- |
| `most-recent` (default) | Deletes an unclaimed earlier round; the newest survives |
| `sequenced` | Drops none; queued rounds dispatch one at a time |
| `idempotent-queue` | Drops a round whose resolved inputs are byte-identical to the most recent prior round |
| `idempotent-settled` | The same comparison, extended to the most-recently-settled successful run |

Under the default, a node that receives two rounds in quick succession runs once, on the newer inputs. Under either idempotent mode, a round that resolves to the same bytes is dropped on purpose. If you need every round, declare `cascade_mode: sequenced` — and read the ordering caveat in [Iterative convergence](iterative-convergence.md) before you rely on the order.

**Every mode compares only within the current frame.** No mode reads a prior frame's run.

## 6. Did the sender run at all in this frame?

A receiver that reads `{{nodes.<sender>.attribute.<key>}}` needs the sender to have produced a value in this run-scope. `force_upstream_refresh` on the subscription decides whether the receiver's invalidation pulls the sender in:

- `force_upstream_refresh: true` invalidates the sender so it re-runs in the same frame **before** this node dispatches. The receiver then carries the value the sender just produced.
- `force_upstream_refresh: false` leaves the sender where it is. When the sender never ran in this frame, the receiver settles with `template_resolution_failed`, because its source had no value.

There is no default. The key is required and registration fails without it, so this is always a choice you made.

## 7. Is the instance paused?

```
curl -s "$API/v1/instances/$ID" | jq '.paused'
```

A paused instance stops the supervisor claiming new dispatches for it. Resume it:

```
curl -X POST "$API/v1/instances/$ID/resume"
```

## 8. Force it, when you have to

Two moves make a node run again.

**Open a fresh frame.** Send a message. Every structural root wakes on an empty message, and the frame that opens carries no memory of the prior one:

```
curl -X POST "$API/v1/instances/$ID/messages" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: $(uuidgen)" -d '{}'
```

**Invalidate the node directly.** The debug-override channel invalidates one node by type:

```
curl -X POST "$API/v1/instances/$ID/debug/override" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"action": "invalidate_node", "node_type": "worker"}'
```

The instance must be **paused or holding an unresumed pause-mode breakpoint hit**; any other state answers `409` naming those two. The same channel sets one attribute with `{"action": "set_attribute", "node_type": "worker", "attribute_key": "retries", "attribute_value": 3}`.

An invalidate against a node whose run is **in flight** queues rather than replaces: the running run stays running and settles normally, a second run appears in `stale`, and it dispatches after the first settles. Both runs happen. That is the sealing rule — an in-flight run is never re-substituted underneath the executor.

## Sharp edges

**Attributes reset outside the run-scope, by design.** A node cascading to itself inside one frame sees each dispatch carry what the previous dispatch wrote. A second operator message opens a second frame and the node begins again at the schema's defaults. A fan-out child also starts at the defaults, and does not continue a sibling's values. A node that "lost" its value across a new message did not fail — it started a new run-scope.

**A `pass` upstream does not emit `terminal/success`.** Where an upstream routes an error class to `action: pass`, its run settles fresh but the settling signal still names the error class. A receiver subscribed to `terminal/success` does not fire. Subscribe to `terminal/*` when you want it to.

**`admin reset` resets one node and nothing else.** It is not a deployment wipe and it asks for no confirmation. Template, instance, and tag counts are unchanged, and no dispatch happens.

**Node tags select over HTTP only.** `GET /v1/instances/{id}/nodes?tag=<value>` filters by node tag. No CLI verb that lists nodes accepts `--tag` or `--tag-prefix`, and `rimsky instance nodes -o json` does not print the tags at all. Where those flags exist they select a different noun: `--tag` on `template register` attaches a **template** tag, and `--tag-prefix` on `template list` filters templates — so reaching for it after tagging nodes filters templates and returns a plausible empty answer.

**A parked node is not a stale node.** Check the park roster before you conclude a node did not wake — see [Diagnosing a stuck instance](journey-stuck-instance.md).
